lessons.title: The Cash Flow Cycle: How Money Moves In and Out of a Business

children.text: Lesson 1.1 showed that profit and cash are different. This lesson shows you the machine that creates the difference. In every business, cash goes out first, travels through stock and work and invoices, and comes back later as more cash. Managing cash is really about managing that loop: how long it takes, how much money it swallows, and where it can jam.

body.text: Cash does not sit still in a business. It goes round in a loop. Every rupee you spend leaves the bank, turns into stock, then into an invoice, then waits, and only then comes back. Your job is to make that loop shorter and cheaper.

children.text: Follow One Order All the Way Round

Anjali runs Urban Threads, a fictional Bengaluru label that makes women's clothing and supplies boutiques. A boutique chain orders 1,000 dresses at ₹1,200 each, so the invoice will be ₹12 lakh. Here is what actually happens to her bank balance.

body.title: One order, one trip around the cash loop

events.title: Order confirmed, fabric bought
events.description: Anjali buys ₹5 lakh of fabric and trims. The mill gives her 40 days of credit, so no cash leaves the bank today. A purchase, not a payment.

events.title: Job work paid: ₹2 lakh out
events.description: The tailoring unit finishes stitching and is paid on delivery. This is the first rupee to actually leave the bank.

events.title: Dispatch and invoice: ₹12 lakh of revenue, ₹0 of cash
events.description: The dresses ship and the invoice goes out. Revenue and profit are recorded today. The bank balance does not move.

events.title: Overheads paid: ₹1 lakh out
events.description: Studio rent, electricity and the salary of her full-time assistant for the period.

events.title: Fabric mill paid: ₹5 lakh out
events.description: The 40 days of supplier credit run out. Cumulative cash out is now ₹8 lakh, all of it funded by Anjali.

events.title: Customer pays: ₹12 lakh in
events.description: The boutique chain settles the invoice 45 days after it was raised. The loop closes and the cash comes home with ₹4 lakh of profit on top.

stats.label: Profit on the order
stats.context: ₹12 lakh billed minus ₹8 lakh of costs

stats.label: Cash Anjali funded
stats.context: Paid out before a single rupee came in

stats.label: Days of funding
stats.context: First payment on Day 20, collection on Day 70

body.text: Notice that the two moments everyone celebrates, winning the order on Day 0 and shipping it on Day 25, produce no cash at all. The bank balance only moves on Day 20, Day 30, Day 40 and Day 70. Sales teams work on the first calendar. Your bank works on the second.

body.title: Shorten the loop
body.prompt: Anjali renegotiates with the boutique chain: payment 30 days after invoice instead of 45. The invoice still goes out on Day 25, and her payments on Days 20, 30 and 40 are unchanged. How many days of funding does the order now need, counting from her first cash payment to the day the customer pays?
body.explanation: The customer now pays on Day 25 plus 30, which is Day 55. Her first outflow is still Day 20, so she funds the order for 55 minus 20, or 35 days, instead of 50. Fifteen days less credit given to the customer came straight off her funding need, with no change to profit.

children.text: Every rupee entering or leaving a business comes through one of three doors. Indian companies report exactly these three buckets in their cash flow statement, and you will use the same split when you build a forecast in Chapter 4.

body.caption: The three activities, with everyday Indian examples

cells: Customer receipts, cash sales, GST refunds
Supplier payments, wages, rent, PF, GST, advance tax
Whether the core business funds itself
Sale of an old machine or vehicle, maturity of a fixed deposit
New machinery, land, computers, deposits placed
What the business is building or selling off
Term loan disbursed, promoter capital, fresh equity
Loan principal repaid, interest, dividends, lease payments
Who is funding the gap, and at what cost

body.label: Where the three buckets come from
body.context: The accounting standards on the statement of cash flows require Indian companies to classify every cash movement as operating, investing or financing. It is not a management convention, it is the statutory format you will see in every annual report filed with the NSE and BSE.

body.text: An EMI is split across two doors. The interest portion is an expense that reduces profit, while the principal portion is a financing outflow that never touches the profit and loss statement. A company can therefore show a healthy profit and still be squeezed dry by principal repayments.

body.title: Which door?
body.question: Urban Threads repays ₹5 lakh of term loan principal and pays ₹40,000 of interest in the same month. How is this classified in the cash flow statement?
options: The whole ₹5.4 lakh is an operating outflow
Neither is a cash flow, because the loan was already recorded when it was taken
The ₹5 lakh principal is a financing outflow, and interest paid is disclosed separately and classified consistently, usually financing for a company
The whole ₹5.4 lakh is an investing outflow
body.explanation: Principal repayment is always financing. Interest paid is shown as a separate line and classified consistently from year to year, usually financing for a company and often operating for a bank or NBFC. The practical point holds either way: only the interest reduces profit, while both reduce cash.

body.title: Classify the van
body.textWithBlank: Buying a delivery van for cash is an ___ activity in the cash flow statement.
body.explanation: Buying a long-term asset is an investing outflow. Only the depreciation on that van later appears as an operating expense in the profit and loss statement.

children.text: Cash leaves a business through a small number of large pipes. For most Indian product businesses, raw material and people dominate, and everything else is noise by comparison.

body.title: Urban Threads: a typical month of cash outflows (%)

children.text: If you want to fix cash, work on the big slices. Squeezing a 2% discount out of a courier partner feels productive, but negotiating 15 extra days from the fabric mill is worth many times more.

body.title: What if the business has no inventory at all?

children.text: A services business, an IT firm, a consultancy or an agency, runs the same loop with one stage removed. There is no raw material and no stock, but people are paid every month whether or not clients have paid.
salaries go out on the 1st, with TDS due by the 7th and PF by the 15th of the following month.
the invoice goes out at the end of the month, or worse, only after the client signs off on a milestone.
the client pays 45, 60 or even 120 days later.
The loop is shorter, but far less flexible. You can delay a fabric purchase. You cannot delay payroll.

columns.label: Product business (Urban Threads)
points: Cash locked in raw material and finished stock
Supplier credit absorbs part of the gap
Purchasing can be paused when cash is tight
Risk: unsold stock that no discount can clear

columns.label: Services business (an IT firm)
points: Cash locked in salaries and unbilled work
Almost no supplier credit to lean on
Risk: a large client stretching payment while the team still has to be paid

children.text: The Loop Speeds Up and Slows Down Through the Year

Indian businesses rarely have a flat year. Festive demand, the monsoon, harvest cycles and the March year end all bend the loop. Urban Threads builds stock through August and September for Diwali, and only sees that cash return in November and December.

body.title: Urban Threads: cash in vs cash out through the festive season (₹ lakh)

children.text: August and September are the dangerous months. The business is spending heavily on fabric and job work for a season that has not started selling yet. A festive stock-out costs one sale. Running out of cash in September costs the whole quarter.

body.title: The bulk discount offer
body.scenario: Urban Threads normally buys ₹5 lakh of fabric a month on 40 days of credit. The mill offers a deal: buy six months of fabric in one go and take 10% off the ₹30 lakh order, but pay within 15 days. Anjali has an overdraft facility costing 11% a year. Procurement is thrilled about saving ₹3 lakh.
body.prompt: Work through the cash effect. Would you approve it?
body.modelAnswer:
Start with the numbers.
1. The discount saves ₹3 lakh on a ₹30 lakh order, so she pays ₹27 lakh.
2. That ₹27 lakh is consumed evenly over six months, so on average roughly ₹27 lakh is tied up for about three months. At 11%, the interest cost is about ₹27,00,000 x 0.11 x 0.25, which is ₹74,250.
3. On finance cost alone, ₹3 lakh saved against roughly ₹74,000 of interest looks like a good deal.
Now the questions the spreadsheet does not answer.
4. Does she have ₹27 lakh of headroom within 15 days, on top of wages, rent and GST? A discount is worthless if it makes payroll bounce.
5. This is fashion. Six months of one season's fabric can become dead stock if designs or colours move on, and there is no discount that rescues dead stock.
6. Storage, damage and the design team changing direction all sit on top of that.
7. A middle path: ask for the same discount on a three-month commitment with staggered deliveries and staggered payment, keeping most of the saving and all of the flexibility.

body.title: Map your own company's loop
steps: Write down your company's three largest cash inflows and who controls their timing.
Write down the five largest outflows and the exact date each one hits the bank.
Mark the outflows on a fixed statutory calendar that cannot be moved, such as TDS by the 7th, PF by the 15th and GST by the 20th.
For one recent order or project, note the date of the first cash outflow and the date the customer actually paid.
Count the days between those two dates. That is how long your business funds its own work.
Ask one question: who funds that gap today, the promoter, a bank limit or the suppliers?

body.title: The Cash Flow Cycle: Key Terms

cards.definition: Cash from the core business: customer receipts in, supplier payments, wages and taxes out.
Cash spent on or received from long-term assets such as machines, vehicles and deposits.
Cash from and to lenders and owners: loans, principal repayments, capital and dividends.
The journey from cash to stock to invoice and back to cash. The longer it runs, the more funding the business needs.
Time a supplier allows before payment. Free funding for the buyer, and a cash cost to the seller.
Work already done and already paid for in salaries, but not yet invoiced to the client.

points: Cash travels in a loop: out to suppliers and staff, into stock and invoices, and back only when the customer pays.
Winning an order and shipping it move no cash. Only payments and collections do.
Every cash movement is operating, investing or financing, the same three buckets used in the statutory cash flow statement.
Only loan interest hits profit. Loan principal is a financing outflow that quietly drains cash.
Fix the big pipes first. Supplier terms and payroll timing move far more cash than small cost savings.
Seasonal buildup is the most dangerous part of the loop, because spending peaks months before collections do.

body.text: Urban Threads is a fictional business used for illustration. Statutory due dates are simplified and can change. Confirm current requirements with your chartered accountant or finance team.
